column3: It almost exactly joins denial of the Hour with confidence of a favorable return to the Lord.
It contrasts a good promise and final presence with temporary worldly enjoyment, qualifying the focus's confident expectation.
Return to God and being informed of one's deeds supplies the focus's final-accounting horizon.
After harm, received ease becomes self-satisfied boasting, closely paralleling the focus's possessive response to mercy.
The immediately preceding verse establishes the same human collapse under harm that the focus develops after relief.
Claiming good fortune as one's own while misattributing evil exposes the same asymmetric attribution behind "this is mine."
Mercy after harm produces corrupt response and is followed by a record of deeds, closely matching the focus's sequence.
Its rule that deeds return upon their doer directly clarifies the focus's threatened report and punishment.
The command to taste what one did supplies a concrete form for the focus's retributive punishment.
Even a slight touch of punishment elicits admission of wrongdoing, anticipating the focus's final exposure of disbelievers.
The beauty of God's names does not clarify relief, presumptuous ownership, the Hour, or accounting.
Universal ownership and return to God give only a broad counterpoint to the focus's claimed favorable return.
Mercy withdrawn produces despair and ingratitude, completing the unstable human response to changing conditions in the focus.
The following verse reverses the circumstances: ease produces withdrawal, while harm produces expansive prayer.
Tasting the touch of Saqar makes the focus's threatened experience of punishment bodily and immediate.
A lesser punishment meant to induce return contrasts with the focus's later, severe consequence for continued disbelief.
Forgiveness and painful punishment form a nearby theological backdrop without developing the focus's particular presumption.
Return to the Knower of the unseen and disclosure of deeds parallels the focus's announced report of actions.
Disbelief in resurrection after death helps frame the focus's dismissal of the Hour.
Succession after Noah's people does not add to the focus's response to mercy or final judgment.
People call upon God in harm but associate partners after receiving mercy, a close counterpart to the focus's misuse of relief.
Mercy rescues believers from severe punishment, contrasting the focus's recipient of mercy who turns presumptuous.
Dispute over revelation and delayed judgment provide local context but little about the focus's claims after mercy.
It asks what fabricators expect on the Day of Resurrection, directly challenging the focus's ungrounded confidence about it.
Rejection of signs is a general disbelief theme and does not explain the focus's particular assertion.
The inviolability of revelation does not illuminate the focus's relief, Hour denial, or recompense.
Divine mercy identifies the source of the mercy in the focus, but adds no detail to the human response.
Received mercy brings joy while adversity is tied to prior deeds, closely framing the focus's relief and ensuing accountability.
Possession of the unseen is denied, challenging the focus's unsupported certainty about a privileged future.
The inability of false gods to avert harm is only an indirect counterpart to the focus's response to harm and mercy.
Brief enjoyment followed by severe punishment qualifies the focus's confidence that present favor guarantees future good.
Future signs will make truth manifest, a local answer to disbelief but not to the focus's proprietary claim.
Standing before the Lord on the Day of Resurrection supplies the meeting and judgment the focus discounts.
Those who do not expect meeting with God reject revelation, providing only a broad parallel to denial of the Hour.
Knowledge of the Hour belongs to God, directly countering the focus's speculative denial of its standing.
The warning of severe punishment and promise of good reward are too general after more direct judgment cards.
A recipient explicitly credits God's favor and is tested by gratitude, a corrective contrast to claiming mercy as personal property.
Repentance and reform after ignorant wrongdoing offer a distant alternative to the focus's unrepentant presumption.
The consequences of tasting the forbidden tree do not clarify the focus's mercy, Hour, or final accounting.
The garden owner's confidence that his possession will not perish prepares the presumptuous posture voiced more fully in 18:36.
It makes rejection of revelation the local condition behind the focus's threatened judgment.
Expectation of meeting one's account is a direct faithful contrast to the focus's denial of the Hour.
Merciful leadership and consultation do not materially clarify the focus's misuse of received mercy.
The joy of believers in the Garden is only a distant contrast to the focus's assumed favorable outcome.
Death followed by return to the Lord establishes the return invoked hypothetically in the focus.
Mocking delayed punishment before its unavoidable arrival qualifies the focus's dismissal of final consequence.
The call to uprightness and forgiveness is a nearby alternative to disbelief, but does not explain the focus's claim.
The Fire as the destination of disbelievers supplies a concise consequence horizon for the focus's severe punishment.
Rules for conduct in battle do not add to the focus's eschatological accounting.
The same pattern of favor producing withdrawal and harm producing despair closely parallels the local sequence around the focus.
The return to God who discloses deeds directly supports the focus's promised report of what was done.
Disbelievers return to God and are informed of their deeds, closely matching the focus's closing warning.
The gathering of God's enemies to the Fire supplies immediate surah context for the focus's final punishment.
Every blessing is from God, and hardship turns people back to Him, directly correcting the focus's claim of ownership.
It vividly depicts inescapable painful punishment, sharpening the focus's warning of a severe torment.
The dispatch of a command from God does not clarify the focus's human response to mercy.
Return and disclosure of deeds repeat the accounting theme with little further connection to the focus.
Wealth and children do not secure nearness to God, directly qualifying the focus's certainty of having the best with Him.
The same surah explicitly promises disbelievers severe punishment and recompense for their deeds.
Cowardice and harsh speech in battle do not illuminate the focus's relief-to-presumption pattern.
A prophet's receipt of mercy from God does not clarify the recipient's possessive response in the focus.
Disbelief returns against its doer while good work prepares for the self, reinforcing personal moral consequence.
The secure station of the God-conscious is only a general contrast to the focus's assumed good standing.
The sudden arrival of the Hour or a barren day's punishment directly bears on the focus's doubt about the Hour.
The actual promise of the Garden belongs to those who affirm God and remain upright, contrasting with the focus's unsupported assurance.
Failure to stand or defend oneself does not clarify the focus's future return or punishment.
The ruling on cutting or leaving date palms is unrelated to the focus's judgment scene.
Admission into mercy for a righteous man offers only a broad contrast to the focus's wrongful use of mercy.
Tasting punishment for disbelief supplies a direct but already well-established form of the focus's final threat.
Joseph credits God's kindness for deliverance, a distant corrective to treating benefit as one's own.
The Fire as lasting recompense for rejecting signs gives the focus's punishment an immediate surah destination.
Tasting evil and great punishment because of one's conduct reinforces the focus's deed-linked retribution.
The announcement of Isaac and Jacob does not add to the focus's mercy or final judgment.
Calling for evil as though it were good offers a remote parallel to disordered human desire.
The Garden's adornment does not clarify the focus's presumptuous claim to the best outcome.
After judgment, Satan disowns those who followed him and directs blame back to them, clarifying final personal accountability.
What the faithful may rightly claim in the hereafter contrasts with the focus's unsupported claim of privileged standing.
Calling upon what can neither harm nor benefit is only indirectly related to the focus's response to hardship.
The Hour's knowledge belongs to God and all return to Him, directly countering the focus's doubt and presumption.
Rejection followed by eventual knowledge gives only a minimal consequence parallel.
The command to arise and warn does not add to the focus's inner response or final reckoning.
Dispute over messengership and testimony does not clarify the focus's mercy or future claim.
Created beings testify at return to God, giving a local mechanism for the focus's disclosure of deeds.
The command to seek forgiveness provides a broad alternative but not the focus's late judgment scene.
A devout community's night worship does not clarify the focus's argument.
Seeking human approval while God refuses the defiantly disobedient is a limited contrast to false confidence in divine favor.
Acknowledging the Lord's decree and tasting punishment parallels the focus's final retributive outcome.
The two good outcomes for believers weakly contrasts with the focus's self-assured claim to the best outcome.
Earth's provisions and measure do not illuminate the focus's relief, Hour, or accountability.
Association nullifies deeds and leads to loss, qualifying the focus's confidence despite disbelief.
Worldly gain accompanied by easy assumptions of forgiveness closely parallels the focus's entitlement and confidence in future favor.
Ranks among those favored for obedience give only a distant contrast to the focus's assumed favor.
Mockery of the messenger and disbelief in the Merciful do not specifically clarify the focus.
Returning disputes to God and the Messenger is too general to illuminate the focus's eschatological return.
The final knowledge of the Hour belongs to the Lord, concisely limiting the focus's speculation about it.
Universal return, just recompense, and painful punishment for disbelief directly gather the focus's final themes.
Satan's abandonment of one he led into disbelief gives only an indirect accountability counterpart.
At death, disbelievers are made to taste burning punishment, concretizing the focus's threatened torment.
Marriage-law provisions do not clarify the focus's mercy, Hour, or judgment.
Trust in the Mighty, Merciful One is a broad corrective to self-reliant presumption but adds little detail.
After harm, a person calls on God, then claims the granted favor came through personal knowledge; this is the closest parallel to the focus's entitlement.
Qarun attributes his wealth to personal knowledge, directly exposing the self-crediting logic behind "this is mine."
People rejoice when mercy touches them and despair when evil follows their own acts, closely matching the focus's response to changing conditions.
It records the claim that the Hour is only conjecture, directly paralleling the focus's denial of its certainty.
Those in punishment acknowledge repeated death and life, confess their sins, and ask whether an exit remains.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out so they can act righteously, providing the focus's final threat with its explicit failed response.
Guilty people before their Lord ask to be sent back to do good, directly contrasting with the focus's confident claim about a future return.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to return in order to act righteously, exposing the belated reversal absent from the focus's presumption.
Harm prompts invocation, while subsequent favor produces turning away and association, a close expansion of the focus's unstable response.
In peril people call on God alone, then turn away after rescue, paralleling the focus's misuse of relief.
A person calls in distress but passes on after relief as though no call had been made, clarifying the forgetfulness behind entitlement.
When God removes harm, some immediately associate partners, showing another corrupt response to received relief.
A person reads honor and provision as a personal verdict of divine favor, qualifying the focus's certainty of the best standing.
Those facing the Fire wish they could return and act differently, supplying a concrete reversal of the focus's unsupported confidence.
When the outcome arrives, people ask whether they can return to act otherwise, directly framing belated recognition at judgment.
The opened record exposes every deed, closely supporting the focus's announced disclosure of what disbelievers did.
Return to God followed by full repayment for every soul's earning gives a concise account of the focus's final recompense.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers all for the Day without doubt, directly opposing the focus's uncertainty about the Hour.
At the approach of death, a person asks for delay to give charity, a practical counterpart to late regret before final accounting.
The people in the Fire ask its keepers to seek a reduction of punishment, extending the focus's severe-torment horizon.
The keepers answer that clear messengers had already come, locating final punishment after rejected warning.
The claim that there is only worldly life and no resurrection gives a direct form of the focus's denial of the Hour.
The emphatic denial that God will raise the dead directly contests the focus's final-return horizon.
The assertion that people will not be resurrected closely parallels the focus's dismissal of the Hour.
Disbelievers claim they will never be raised, followed by an oath that they will be informed of their deeds.
Disbelief in being remade after becoming dust gives a direct resurrection objection relevant to the focus's future return.
The objection to becoming a new creation after bones and dust supplies another explicit form of resurrection denial.
The challenge over who revives decayed bones directly addresses the return and resurrection the focus treats as uncertain.
The question whether scattered bones will be gathered gives a concise resurrection challenge behind the focus's claim.
